subject: MATHS
name: Squares and Square Roots
summary: Perfect squares, the patterns they follow, and getting back out again.
source: NCERT Class 8 Mathematics, syllabus topic coverage only

questions.solution: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself: 12 × 12 = 144. The distractor 121 is 11², which is the usual slip — the squares of consecutive numbers sit close together, and 121 and 144 are only 23 apart.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is a perfect square?
questions.solution: A perfect square is a number you get by squaring a whole number. 49 = 7 × 7, so it qualifies. None of 50, 51 or 52 can be written that way — the next perfect square after 49 is 64, so nothing between them is one.

questions.stem: A perfect square can never end in which of these digits?
questions.solution: Square the digits 0 to 9 and look at the last digit of each: 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1. Only 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and 9 ever appear. So a number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 cannot be a perfect square — and that is a one-second test you can apply before doing any work at all.

questions.stem: How many whole numbers lie strictly between 9² and 10²?
questions.solution: 9² = 81 and 10² = 100, so the numbers strictly between them run from 82 to 99, which is 18 numbers. The general rule is that between n² and (n+1)² there are exactly 2n numbers — here 2 × 9 = 18. Note it is 2n and not 2n+1, because both endpoints are excluded.

questions.stem: What is the square root of 1024?
questions.solution: By prime factorisation, 1024 = 2¹⁰. Pairing the factors gives 2⁵ = 32, so √1024 = 32. Check it the other way: 32 × 32 = 1024. Note that 30² = 900 and 40² = 1600, so the answer had to lie between 30 and 40 before any factorising began.

questions.stem: What is the square root of 6.25?
questions.solution: Write 6.25 as 625/100. Then √(625/100) = 25/10 = 2.5. Decimals trip people up because the answer is smaller than you expect: 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25, and squaring a number between 1 and 10 that has one decimal place gives one with two.

questions.stem: What is the smallest number by which 252 must be multiplied to make it a perfect square?
questions.solution: Factorise: 252 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 7. The 2s pair up and the 3s pair up, but the 7 is alone. Multiplying by 7 gives it a partner, and 252 × 7 = 1764 = 42². The method is always the same — factorise, find the unpaired primes, and multiply by their product.

questions.stem: A square garden has an area of 1225 m². What is the length of one side?
questions.solution: For a square, area = side², so side = √1225. Factorising, 1225 = 5 × 5 × 7 × 7, which pairs to 5 × 7 = 35. So each side is 35 m. A quick sanity check: 35² = 1225, and 30² = 900 with 40² = 1600, so 35 sits sensibly between them.

questions.stem: What is the least number that must be subtracted from 1000 to make it a perfect square?
questions.solution: Find the largest perfect square not exceeding 1000. Since 31² = 961 and 32² = 1024, which overshoots, the answer is 961. So subtract 1000 − 961 = 39. The common error is to subtract to reach 1024 instead, but that would mean adding 24, not subtracting — read whether the question asks you to add or take away.

questions.stem: What is the square root of 15129?
questions.solution: Use the last digit and the size together. The number ends in 9, so its root ends in 3 or 7. It lies between 120² = 14400 and 130² = 16900, so the root is in the 120s. That leaves 123 or 127. Since 125² = 15625 is already too big, the root must be below 125, so it is 123. Checking, 123 × 123 = 15129.

The sum of the first n odd numbers is exactly n². Here the last term is 39, and the odd numbers run 1, 3, 5, …, so 39 is the 20th of them (since the nth odd number is 2n − 1, and 2 × 20 − 1 = 39). The sum is therefore 20² = 400. This identity is worth knowing on sight: it is why the gaps between consecutive perfect squares are the odd numbers.

questions.stem: What is the smallest perfect square that is divisible by each of 4, 9 and 10?
questions.solution: First find the LCM, since the number must be a multiple of all three: LCM(4, 9, 10) = 180. Now 180 = 2² × 3² × 5, and the 5 is unpaired, so 180 is not itself a square. Multiply by 5 to pair it: 900 = 2² × 3² × 5² = 30². The distractor 3600 is also a perfect square divisible by all three, but it is not the smallest — which is what the question asks.
